examples.problem_statement: x is a digit in the decimal 12.15x9, which, if rounded to the nearest hundredth, would equal 12.16. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 4. Choose whether Quantity A is greater, Quantity B is greater, the two quantities are equal, or the relationship cannot be determined.

solution.result: the digit that decides the rounding is x, sitting in the thousandths place
solution.description: Locate the hundredths digit (5) and see that the digit immediately to its right, which controls whether that 5 stays or rounds up, is x.
Because the decimal rounds up from 12.15 to 12.16, the thousandths digit x must be 5 or greater, leaving only the digits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.

solution.result: every allowed value of x exceeds 4, so Quantity A is greater
solution.description: Test each surviving possibility for x against Quantity B; since all of them are greater than 4, the comparison is settled in favour of Quantity A.

key_reminders: A decimal rounds up at a given place only when the digit immediately to its right is 5 or more.
Digits further right than the deciding digit (here the final 9) do not change the rounding decision.
A quantitative comparison is determined when every value allowed by the constraints falls on the same side.
common_mistakes: Letting the trailing 9 of 12.15x9 drive the rounding instead of x, the digit directly after the hundredths place.
Reading x \ge 5 as x > 5 and dropping the case x = 5.
Choosing (D) on the grounds that x is not a single fixed value, even though all admissible values give the same comparison.

concept.technique_name: sum of triangular numbers via series decomposition

examples.problem_statement: Find the sum of 20 terms of the series 3 + 6 + 10 + 15 + \ldots

solution.result: each given term is a running sum of consecutive integers, i.e. a triangular number
solution.description: Rewrite the listed terms as sums of consecutive integers to expose that the series is made of triangular numbers, just starting one step in.

solution.result: the required sum equals the sum of 21 terms of the full triangular series, less 1
solution.description: Prepend the missing first triangular number 1 so the series begins at its natural start, which adds one term, then subtract that 1 back out to keep the value unchanged.

solution.result: a closed form for the n-th term of the completed series
solution.description: Replace each bracketed run of consecutive integers with the standard formula for the sum of the first n integers, so the series can be summed term-formula-wise.
Add the closed-form terms over the 21 terms of the completed series to get the total the book reports for that extended sum.
Remove the 1 that was inserted in step 2 to return to the sum of the 20 terms actually asked for.

key_reminders: Adding a missing leading term to make a series regular is legitimate only if the same amount is subtracted back.
Padding the series to its natural start shifts the term count: 20 asked-for terms become 21 terms of the completed series.
common_mistakes: Summing 20 terms of the completed series instead of 21, forgetting that inserting the leading 1 shifted the index.
Adding the 1 back at the end instead of subtracting it.
Treating 3, 6, 10, 15 as an arithmetic progression because the first two gaps look regular, when the differences 3, 4, 5 are themselves increasing.

examples.problem_statement: Approximation during multiplication is sensitive: a small change in the multiplier or multiplicand can badly skew the result, so the common trick of increasing one factor and decreasing the other should be avoided when the answer choices are close together. Find the approximate value of 384 \times 299. Choices: 1) 1,14,000  2) 1,15,000  3) 1,16,000

solution.result: the naive rounding lands on 114000, off by 816 from the true product
solution.description: Try the widely used shortcut of nudging one factor up and the other down first, and see that its answer deviates enough to pick the wrong choice when the options are close.

solution.result: each factor is split into a round base plus a small signed change
solution.description: Shift each factor to the nearest convenient multiple of ten and record the leftover as a signed correction, writing +4 under 380 and -1 under 300.

solution.result: a base product plus a cross-correction row
solution.description: Expand the product so the easy base term 380 \times 300 sits on the first row and the cross terms formed by the two corrections make the second row.
Evaluate the correction row roughly rather than exactly, discarding the tiny product of the two corrections, since only an approximate value is wanted.
Add the correction row to the base product from the first row to obtain the sharpened estimate.
Round the sharpened estimate to the nearest listed choice, which the naive method could not distinguish from 1,14,000.

key_reminders: Shift each factor to the nearest (highest possible) power of ten and carry the leftover as a signed correction.
(a + p)(b + q) = ab + pb + qa + pq, and the correction row pb + qa carries the deviation.
The correction row is meant to be estimated roughly; the pq term is small enough to neglect.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 380 \times 300 = 1,14,000 and picking choice 1, which is exactly the trap the deviation creates.
Getting the sign of the 299 correction wrong and adding 1 \times 380 instead of subtracting it, which pushes the estimate towards 1,16,000.
Computing the correction row exactly and losing the speed advantage the method exists for.
